# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
# Review: Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

**Bottom line:** the comment's re-analysis (sections 1–4) is valuable and mostly sound. It uncovers a factual misstatement in the Halden paper about when organisations withdrew, and it shows the output and hours corrections with clear arithmetic. However, the final conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is not supported by the comment's own evidence:
- After correction, the comment still finds a gain of about 11% per hour.
- The randomised Varden case-processing result found a similar gain under exactly the conditions the comment recommends.
- The novelty argument that is meant to explain away the remaining gain is never tested, even though the data to test it exist.
- The section on the Varden meetings hypothesis misrepresents that paper.

## What checks out

| Check | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 | −2.6% ✓ |

**Two figures that don't reconcile:**

- **The parts of the hours increase add up to more than the total.**
  - Four days at +0.7 hours is 2.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours on the day off gives 4.4 extra hours on top of the 32 scheduled, about **36.4 hours per week**.
  - The reported pilot average is **34.6**, so about 2 hours are unexplained.
  - Perhaps the +0.7 is measured from a different baseline, or the two components cover different sets of organisations. Either way, the paper needs to explain how the parts reconcile with the total.
- **The novelty extrapolation.** Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 SD per month. Continuing that line reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten". The difference is small, but the point it supports is already speculative (see section 3 below).

---

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own evidence

The comment calls the Varden trial "the most reliable finding in the literature". It then cites only the counter-office result. But the Varden case-processing offices were studied under exactly the conditions the comment recommends:
- random assignment,
- output from administrative records,
- actual hours from timesheets,
- nine months of follow-up, longer than Halden's six.

They found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**.

The comment's own corrected estimate is **+10.8%**. Two independent sources, one randomised and one corrected observational, land within two points of each other. That is evidence *for* a real gain per hour of roughly 10–12% in work that doesn't depend on staff being present. It is not evidence that the gain is "entirely an artifact".

The claim also sits awkwardly with the wider literature on long hours and declining productivity per hour (e.g., Pencavel, 2015, *Economic Journal*), which the comment doesn't address.

The Abstract also contradicts itself. It first says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain", which fits the evidence. It then says they account for the gain "entirely", which does not.

## 2. Attrition is documented but never corrected

The finding about withdrawals is important. If seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began, and most cited problems with workload, the Halden paper's "preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons" is a material misstatement. The Halden authors should respond.

However:
- **The Abstract misdescribes Table 2.** It says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. Attrition is the first problem, but Table 2 corrects only the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition is not corrected at all.
- **The likely size of the attrition bias can be bounded, and it is modest.** Suppose the nine withdrawn organisations were of average size (about 48 employees each) and had output of 85 (a severe assumption). Adding them back moves the pooled index from 98.7 to about **97.0**. Applying a similar 2-point reduction to the 17-organisation subset gives roughly 93.4 / 86.1 ≈ **+8.5%** per hour. That is smaller, but still clearly positive.
- **The microdata may allow a direct check.** If the withdrawn organisations submitted monthly index values before they left, those values should be reported.

## 3. The novelty argument is asserted, not tested

The novelty argument is the step that turns "most" into "entirely", yet it rests on the weakest evidence in the comment:
- **The wrong variable.** It relies on self-reported energy, not output. The Halden index was collected **monthly**, so the microdata can show directly whether output per hour fell between months 1 and 6. That is the test the argument needs, and the comment doesn't run it.
- **Two data points.** A straight line drawn through two points cannot tell decay towards zero from levelling off at a new, higher level. Energy at month 6 (+0.29 SD) is consistent with either.
- **Moving the burden of proof.** The claim that "the burden of proof lies with those claiming [a durable effect]" is a matter of rhetoric, not evidence. The comment's conclusion makes a definite claim (the gain is entirely an artifact), so it carries a burden of proof too.
- **The comment ignores longer evidence.** The Varden case-processing gain was measured at nine months, which is around or past the point at which the comment's own extrapolation puts energy back at baseline.

## 4. Section 7 misrepresents the Varden meetings analysis

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known"** is inaccurate.
  - Varden collected the calendar data in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results were available.
  - The seven offices are *all* the treated case-processing offices, which is a stratum defined before randomisation, not a chosen subgroup.
- **The Varden authors already stated the caveats the comment raises.** They said the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and they registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up. The comment presents these points as its own criticism without acknowledging this.
- **The comment holds the two hypotheses to different standards.** The meetings hypothesis is dismissed as having "outrun its evidence". The novelty hypothesis has weaker support (two survey points, a different outcome, no test against output) but is used to support the comment's central conclusion. The two should be judged by the same standard.
- **The comment leaves out supporting evidence.** The Halden managers' own interviews (47 of 58 mentioned cutting meetings) point in the same direction as Varden. That is weak evidence, but it is relevant.

It is fair to say that r = 0.71 across seven offices is fragile: its 95% interval runs from about −0.09 to 0.95. But the right conclusion is "unconfirmed, awaiting the registered test", not "should not be cited".

## 5. The record-based corrections need caveats and uncertainty

- **Billable hours are a poor measure of output here.** Billable hours fall almost automatically when hours worked fall. If billable-hour firms make up much of the 23 (or 17) organisations, the record-based index understates output in exactly the way that would erase a per-hour gain. Please break down the record types and report the correction without billable-hour firms.
- **Records may not be more valid than the manager's index.** Counts of tickets or units can miss quality or complexity that a manager's judgement might capture. The pattern of 19 out of 23 is suggestive of upward bias in the manager index, but the record-based index is not automatically the truth.
- **No uncertainty is reported anywhere.** The key estimate rests on 17 organisations. The 10.8% needs a confidence interval, as do the 3.8-point gap between manager and record-based output and the retail figure. The retail figure (an 11.2% fall) comes from **three organisations**.
- **The subset problem is acknowledged only in the Data note.** The Data note rightly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The Abstract and Conclusion then generalise to "reduced-hours schemes". Report the sector mix of the 17 organisations. Firms that use time tracking (professional services, software) may differ systematically from the others.
- **No control group, in either direction.** The comment's corrected estimate still has no control group. Economic conditions during the pilot could bias it either way, and the comment doesn't discuss this.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Revenue deflator.** Consumer price inflation is a rough deflator for business revenue, and especially for non-profits. A producer or sector price index would be better, and the source of the 4.1% figure should be cited. The main point still stands: nominal growth of 1.4% is not real growth.
- **The final recommendations are good.** Record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up, and analysis of everyone who enrolled are all sound. Varden already meets most of them, which is one more reason to engage with its case-processing result rather than leave it out.

---

## A conclusion the evidence would support

> Correcting the output measure and the hours denominator reduces the Halden per-hour gain from 23.4% to about 11% in the subset where correction is possible; the attrition bias is not corrected and would plausibly reduce it further. The corrected estimate is close to the randomised Varden case-processing estimate (12.5%), suggesting a real but much smaller per-hour gain in work not bound to presence. Whether it persists beyond the first months remains untested. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output per employee.

That version keeps all four of the comment's valid corrections without overstating the conclusion. It is also more useful to readers, because it brings the evidence from all three papers together rather than dismissing the part that doesn't fit.
